newsitem.title: INDIA: Probe starts into world's worst mid-air collision.
newsitem.headline: Probe starts into world's worst mid-air collision.

text.p: Daylight revealed on Wednesday the full, appalling horror of the world's biggest mid-air disaster in which some 350 people died and Indian villagers said the catastrophe could have been even worse.
They said they believed the pilot of a Saudi Arabian Airlines jumbo which collided with a Kazakh cargo plane somehow managed to avoid crashing on their houses 80 km (50 miles) southwest of New Delhi.

Housewife Krishna Devi said she was cooking dinner at her outdoor kitchen in the village of Kheri Sanwal on Tuesday and saw the flaming Saudi plane crash. "I saw the plane circle this area twice. It was on fire," she said.
She and others said they believed the pilot tried to avoid the houses.

"We believe that the pilot was alive after the collision and directed the airplane to deserted fields, otherwise many of us would have been killed had the debris fallen over the village," United News of India newsagency quoted Karan Singh from the nearby village of Dahani Phogat as saying.
The Indian government has ordered a inquiry into the collision, aviation officials said. Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was to visit the sites later on Wednesday.

Searchers toiled through the darkness on the north Indian plain to pick charred and mangled bodies from the debris after the two aircraft plunged to earth in flames 10 km (six miles) apart on a clear night.
There were 312 people, including women and children aboard the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 which came down in mustard and chickpea fields minutes after taking off for Dhahran and Jeddah.
A Saudi newspaper said they included 215 Indians, 13 Saudis, nine Nepalis and three Pakistanis. The U.S. Embassy in New Delhi said two as yet unidentified American women were on the flight.
British officials said one English woman, Karen McCoy, returning to her job in Saudi Arabia from a holiday in India, was also among the dead.
The bodies were taken away in trucks and tractor-trailers.
The wreckage of the Saudi plane was still smouldering early on Wednesday. The main section of the fuselage, its roof ripped off, was barely recognisable.

Aboard the KazAir Ilyushin IL-76 were 25 businessmen who had chartered the aircraft to fly empty to Delhi. They intended to fill it with Indian woollens for sale back home, KazAir's Delhi airport manager Rajiv Bhaskar said.

There were also two children and 10 crew on the plane and Bhaskar told Reuters at the crash site searchers had found the cockpit voice and flight data recorders in the wreckage of the IL-76 that should explain what happened.
The plane was broken in two and Bhaskar said all 37 bodies, six of them badly charred, had been recovered.

Only the tail section of the Saudi aircraft, carrying mostly Indian workers and pilgrims to the Moslem holy land, was reasonably intact after it plunged into the ground leaving a 20-foot (six-metre) crater.
Seats stood upright, dinner trolleys and unbroken crockery sat forlorn in the fields as rescue workers tramped past suitcases, letters and photographs scattered in the dirt.

Some suitcases were empty and local people said there had been looting. "It's very sad that people here behave in this manner," local businessman Vinod Garg told Reuters as police tried to keep people off the sprawling crash site.
Local governments declared a day of mourning. Schoolgirls said they assembled for a two-minute prayer for the victims and then were sent home.
Civil aviation experts sifted through the debris of the Saudi jumbo searching for its cockpit voice and flight data recorders and other vital clues to one of the world's five worst air disasters.
A variety of possible explanations were on offer, ranging from inadequate equipment at Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of ground controller instructions.
Indian civil aviation officials said the Saudi plane was cleared to climb to 14,000 feet after taking off and the Kazakh freighter had been told to stay at 15,000 feet, a normal separation.
But experts said someone, somewhere made a mistake.

One possibility, they said, was that Delhi's ageing radar could not up pinpoint the altitudes of converging aircraft on the only air corridor to and from an airport in the process of modernising its radars and other safety equipment.

Another was that the pilot of the Kazakh plane may have got wrong instructions given in English, the language of international aviation which several experts said pilots from the former Soviet Union often had difficulty understanding.
